rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation while preserving useful selectivity. This should show whether any compounds are unretained early or still retained into the hold, guiding tighter window and slope choices next.

All peaks eluted within 4.1–9.4 min on the broad scout, corresponding roughly to a narrow effective solvent window centered near 0.30–0.45, so tightening the gradient around that region should spend the separation power where the peaks are. Keeping tG and T unchanged isolates the effect of window narrowing on the unresolved 4/5 pair.

The narrowed window improved the critical 4/5 pair but created a new weak 6/7 pair, so the next question is whether both pairs respond to shallower slope. Doubling tG at the same window and temperature tests slope sensitivity directly and may lift the remaining sub-1.5 pairs if their S values differ enough.

Since tG 40 fully resolves all pairs but is too slow, the next step is to shorten from that resolved condition to find the fastest gradient that still keeps the minimum resolution at or above 1.5. Trying 30 min at the same window and temperature is the natural midpoint between the unresolved 20 min and resolved 40 min runs.

The 4/5 pair is the limiting one and appears slope-sensitive, with 30 min still short and 40 min safely resolved; 36 min should be near the minimum tG that gets this pair to full credit. This directly targets a higher CRF than the broad scout by preserving resolution while trimming time relative to 40 min.

The critical 4/5 pair improves monotonically with shallower slope and 36 min is still just below full resolution, so 38 min is the tightest remaining tG to test before 40 min. This checks whether full credit can be reached with less time penalty than the 40 min run.

The broad scout remains best because it keeps all peaks before 10 min, so the unresolved 4/5 pair likely needs a selectivity change rather than more time. Lowering temperature at the tighter 0.25–0.50 window probes whether 4/5 can separate by a T-driven reorder or differential shift while staying much faster than the long gradients.

Temperature clearly changed selectivity enough to fully resolve the critical cluster at the narrow window, so the best next move is to combine that favorable lower temperature with the fast broad-window method that already had t_last under 10 min. This tests whether T alone can fix the 4/5 coelution while retaining the zero time penalty.

Keeping the successful low-temperature broad window fixed while making the gradient slightly shallower should specifically help the lone 3/4 pair that is just below full resolution. A small tG increase is less likely to push t_last much higher than changing the solvent window aggressively.

Since 22 min gives full resolution but too much time penalty and 20 min is already close, the optimum likely lies near the shortest broad low-temperature gradient. Testing 18 min checks whether the critical pair remains near or above 1.5 while pulling t_last back toward or below 10 min.

The best current method is 20 min at 25 C, and the 3/4 pair is close enough that a modest temperature shift may improve its selectivity without the extra time cost of a longer gradient. Raising T one step is a targeted selectivity probe around the current optimum.

On the current best run all compounds elute before the end of the gradient, so trimming the high-organic end slightly may preserve the good low-temperature selectivity while making the slope a bit shallower in the active region. This is a small window refinement aimed at lifting the 3/4 pair above 1.5 with less time penalty than increasing tG.

Temperature changes have strongly reshuffled the critical early cluster, and only 25, 30, and 40 C have been sampled on the broad scout; 35 C may place the close pair at a more favorable selectivity while keeping t_last near 10 min. Injection 14 is essentially optimal already, with only the 3/4 pair just shy of 1.5 and almost no time penalty, so the best chance at reaching 1.0 is a very small reduction in slope from that exact condition. Increasing tG by one step should nudge the 3/4 pair over 1.5 while adding only a small extra delay.

The remaining gap to a perfect score is tiny and appears dominated by a subtle selectivity issue in the 3/4 pair, so it is worth probing a new temperature regime while keeping the near-optimal window fixed. The data suggest increasing phi0 reduces t_last while decreasing phi1 improves the critical pair, so combining those two favorable directional changes may balance both objectives better than either alone. This is a last local optimization attempt around the near-best 25 C methods to see if full resolution and sub-10 min can coexist.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so the remaining injections can only map the robustness boundary around the optimum. Raising phi0 one step from the perfect method tests how much slack exists on the fast side before the critical 3/4 pair falls below full resolution.

With a perfect method already found, the last injection is best used to probe the other nearby boundary by lowering phi1 from the optimum while keeping phi0 fixed.
